Rabid bats have been documented in 49 continental states, and bats are increasingly recognized as important wildlife reservoirs for rabies virus variants that can be transmitted to humans. 5. Epidemiologic data suggest that rabies virus transmission can occur from minor, seemingly insignificant, or unrecognized bat bites. 6. 7. Human and domestic animal contact with bats should be minimized, and bats should not be handled by untrained or unvaccinated individuals or kept as pets. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. Clustering of bat-associated human rabies cases within the same household has never been reported. 13. 14. 15. PEP may be considered for individuals in the same room as the bat who might be unaware of a bite or direct contact, such as a sleeping person who awakens to find a bat in the room or an unattended child, mentally disabled person, or intoxicated individual in the presence of a bat. 16. PEP is not warranted for other household members in such scenarios. 17. Terrestrial carnivores such as raccoons, skunks, foxes, and coyotes are the most commonly infected wild animals with rabies. 18. 19. If PEP has been started and subsequent testing shows the animal was not rabid, the prophylaxis can be discontinued. 20. Signs of rabies in wildlife cannot be reliably interpreted; therefore, any such animal that exposes a person should be euthanized immediately (without unnecessary damage to the head) and the brain submitted for rabies testing. 21. If testing results are negative for rabies by immunofluorescence, the saliva can be assumed to contain no virus, and the exposed individual does not require PEP. 22. Small rodents (e.g., squirrels, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chipmunks, rats, and mice) and lagomorphs (e.g., rabbits and hares) are almost never found to be infected with rabies and have not been known to transmit rabies to humans. 23. From 1990 to 1996, in areas of the U.S. where raccoon rabies was enzootic, woodchucks accounted for 93% of the 371 reported rabies cases among rodents. 24. In cases involving rodents, the state or local health department should be consulted before deciding to initiate antirabies PEP. 25. Offspring of wild animals crossbred with domestic dogs and cats (wild animal hybrids) are considered wild animals by the National Association of State and Public Health Veterinarians (NASPHV) and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE). 26. Because the period of rabies virus shedding in these hybrids is unknown, they should be euthanized and tested rather than confined and observed when they bite humans. 27. Wild animals and wild animal hybrids should not be kept as pets. 28. Animals maintained in USDA-licensed research facilities or accredited zoological parks should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. 29. The likelihood of rabies in domestic animals varies by region, and the need for PEP also varies accordingly. 30. In the continental U.S., rabies among dogs is most commonly reported along the U.S.-Mexico border and sporadically in areas with enzootic wildlife rabies. 31. During most of the 1990s, more rabid cats than dogs were reported in the U.S., primarily associated with the epizootic of raccoon rabies in the eastern U.S. 32. The high number of rabies-infected cats may be attributed to fewer cat vaccination laws, fewer leash laws, and the roaming habits of cats. 33. 34. Based on new information regarding rabies pathogenesis and viral shedding patterns in ferrets, ferrets are now categorized with dogs and cats rather than as wild terrestrial carnivores. 35. A healthy domestic dog, cat, or ferret that bites a person may be confined and observed for 10 days. 36. Any illness in the animal during confinement or before release should be evaluated by a veterinarian and reported immediately to the local public health department. 37. If signs suggestive of rabies develop, the animal should be euthanized, and its head removed and shipped under refrigeration for examination by a qualified laboratory. 38. If the biting animal is stray or unwanted, it should either be observed for 10 days or euthanized immediately and submitted for rabies examination. 39. An unprovoked attack by an animal is more likely than a provoked attack to indicate that the animal is rabid. 40. Bites inflicted on a person attempting to feed or handle an apparently healthy animal are less likely to indicate rabies.
